questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend defining the capstone task before choosing a model?
options: Because tasks must always be chosen after training is already complete
Because model choice has no bearing on what tasks are feasible
Because a narrow, concretely evaluable task is what makes Chapter 7's evaluation methods usable, and picking a model first tends to lead to vague, unevaluable goals
Because all open-weight models support exactly the same set of tasks
questions.explain: A narrow, one-sentence task with a concrete success metric is what allows building a good eval set. Picking an exciting model first and finding a use for it afterward tends to produce a vague goal that's hard to evaluate.

questions.q: Why is the 1B-8B parameter range described as the practical sweet spot for this capstone?
options: Because the capstone is meant to run on realistic single-GPU hardware with LoRA/QLoRA, and a model too large to train in that setting teaches nothing even if it ranks higher on a leaderboard
Because licensing only permits fine-tuning for models under 8B parameters
Because models above 8B parameters cannot be fine-tuned under any circumstances
Because larger models always perform worse after fine-tuning
questions.explain: The capstone needs to actually finish running on realistic hardware. A model that never completes a training run due to size constraints doesn't provide a usable learning outcome, regardless of its benchmark ranking.

questions.q: What is the key tradeoff between fine-tuning from a raw base model versus an already instruction-tuned checkpoint?
options: There is no difference between the two starting points
Instruction-tuned checkpoints cannot be further fine-tuned at all

A base model gives full control over behavior but needs more data and chat-template setup from scratch, while an instruction-tuned checkpoint converges faster but inherits its existing habits, biases, and verbosity patterns
Base models always produce better results regardless of dataset size
questions.explain: Starting from a base model requires more data and careful setup but offers full control. Continuing from an instruction-tuned checkpoint converges faster for a narrow behavior change but carries over that checkpoint's existing tendencies.

questions.q: Why should a candidate model be sanity-checked (loaded, parameter count verified, chat template inspected) before dataset-building work begins?
options: This step is optional and does not meaningfully affect the project timeline
Because transformers cannot load any model without this exact code pattern
To confirm the model loads correctly, matches expected specs, and produces correctly formatted chat-template output, avoiding a confusing and time-consuming debugging session later
Because parameter counts are always inaccurate in model cards and must be recomputed
questions.explain: A quick sanity check that the model loads, has the expected parameter count, and produces correct chat-template output catches problems early, before significant time is invested in dataset construction.

questions.q: What is the five-lesson pipeline this capstone chapter follows, as laid out in this lesson?
options: Quantization, serving cost estimation, handoff, deployment, and monitoring
Pretraining, tokenization, parallelism, monitoring, and deployment
Only model selection and a final exam, with no hands-on work
Task/model selection, building the SFT dataset, running the fine-tune, evaluating against a baseline, and writing up results
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly lists the pipeline: this lesson covers task framing and model selection, followed by dataset building, fine-tuning, evaluation against baseline, and a final write-up lesson.
